questions.question_text: Mr Archie Collins is a 25-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with schizophrenia. His wife obtains a copy of the correspondences sent to his GP and notes that he has been experiencing 'gedankenlautwerden'. Which of the below best describes this phenomenon?

options.text: Giving answers to questions that are approximately correct
Having a thought inserted into one's mind
Hearing ones thought after thinking it
An individual purposelessly resisting an examiner attempting to move their limbs
Hearing one's thought at the time of thinking it

correct_answer.text: Hearing one's thought at the time of thinking it

correct_answers.text: Hearing one's thought at the time of thinking it

questions.explanation: Gedankenlautwerden is the experience of hearing one's thoughts spoken aloud at the same time they arise in the mind. Écho de la pensée describes the phenomenon of hearing one's thoughts spoken aloud after they have arisen.

questions.question_text: Miss Emily Karenina is a 28-year-old woman who was admitted to an inpatient psychiatric unit after her parents brought her to an A&E. She was reportedly acting oddly for several weeks. She had insisted on covering the windows of her house with wallpaper as she was convinced the she was being watched. On physically examination, she resisted any attempts to move her limbs with the same force that was applied to them. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: This is oppositional paratonia or gegenhalten. The individual affected resists all passive movements with the same degree of force used by the examiner. It is a milder form of negativism wherein the individual does the opposite of what is asked as well as resists passive manipulations.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Vivian Brooke is a 64-year-old woman with a long history of schizophrenia. She has recently been admitted to a general medical unit with an exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease. When asked where she is, she responds by saying "the young doctor's training place". What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: This is most likely to describe circumstantiality, wherein an individual talks or answers questions with excessive and unnecessary detail. They do return to the point, unlike in tangentiality, in which the point is not reached. Verbigeration is a verbal stereotypy in which one or several sentences or strings of words are repeated continuously. Vorbeireden (talking past the point) is seen in Ganser's syndrome; patients will respond to questions in a manner, which shows they understood them, but will provide obviously incorrect answers.

questions.question_text: Mr Jonathan Tonks is a 29-year-old man who shows little inclination to form friendships or other interpersonal connections and tends toward solitary activities. Which of the following personality disorders best describes this behaviour?
questions.explanation: Individuals with a schizoid personality disorder tend to show a lack of interest in social relationships, a tendency towards a solitary or sheltered lifestyle, secretiveness, emotional coldness, detachment, and apathy.

questions.question_text: Borderline personality disorder is associated with a variety of psychological difficulties often leading to distress and maladaptive behaviours. Which of the following is characteristic of borderline personality disorder?

options.text: Insistence on carrying out activities in a certain way

questions.explanation: Borderline personality disorder is characterised by persistent low self-esteem, an unstable self-identity, fears of abandonment, dissociative symptoms and recurrent self-harm.

questions.question_text: Neurasthenia was first described by Van Deusen and Beard in 1869 to denote a condition with symptoms of fatigue, anxiety, headache, heart palpitations, high blood pressure, neuralgia, and depressed mood. Under which of the following headings is it listed in ICD-11?

options.text: Reaction to severe stress, and adjustment disorders

questions.explanation: It was listed under ICD-10 48.0, other neurotic disorders, along with derealisation-depersonalisation disorder. In ICD-11 the term bodily distress disorder replaces ICD-10 somatoform disorders and also includes the concept of ICD-10 neurasthenia. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6313247/

questions.question_text: Adjustment disorder is a collection of depressive and anxiety symptoms that do not meet criteria for other mental disorders, and which occur in association with a stressful event and result in functional impairment. Within what length of time of a stressor do symptoms normally develop in adjustment disorder as per ICD-11?
questions.explanation: IICD-11 states that an adjustment disorder should start within 1 month of a stressor. DSM-5 allows 3 months.

questions.question_text: Mr. Jason Isbell is a 50-year-old man who has been brought to A&E by his family after finding him in a confused state after not hearing from him for a few days. On examination he is disorientated to time and place, perplexed and unwilling to allow examination. Which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: It would be most appropriate to treat this as a case of delirium, given the acute mental state change, disorientation and the presence of confusion.

questions.question_text: Bereavement is a normal life experience, albeit a distressing one. It has been conceptualised by a variety of authors, many of which have described certain stages in the grieving process. Which of the following is not a normal stage of grief?
questions.explanation: The most well known model of grief is that described by Kubler Ross and Kessler which mentioned 5 stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.

questions.question_text: Miss Rosemary Wills is a 30-year-old woman who reports odd experiences, which her mental health team do not believe, are truly psychotic as their characteristics are different to true hallucinations. Which of the following is true of pseudohallucinations?

options.text: Are not present in a normal state
Can be summoned and dismissed at will

questions.explanation: Pseudohallucinations can be difficult to distinguish from true hallucinations, but are commonly described as being "like" the individual is experiencing something. They are often not perceived as objectively occurring for other people, are perceived as negative but are not associated with delusional ideation. They can be present during periods of stability and appear to be commonly auditory, although can occur in other modalities.

questions.question_text: People with personality disorders usually experience difficulties in relating to or interacting with other individuals or society. Which of the following personality disorders is most likely to be associated with individuals being viewed as non-conformist
questions.explanation: Schizotypal personality disorder is characterised by severe social anxiety, thought disorder, paranoid ideation, derealisation, transient psychosis, and unconventional beliefs. People often feel they are simply eccentric, productive, or nonconformist. Many people with personality disorders do exhibit behaviours that are not socially sanctioned but those with schizotypal personality disorder are most usually referred to as eccentric or similar.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Abigail Peterson is a 45-year-old woman who is diagnosed with an adjustment disorder after abruptly being made redundant at work. Which of the following is true of adjustment disorder in DSM 5?

options.text: Medication is the first line treatment
It is not associated with suicidal risk
Symptoms should resolve within 6 months of the stress ending
Symptoms should start within 1 month of a stressor beginning

correct_answer.text: Symptoms should resolve within 6 months of the stress ending

correct_answers.text: Symptoms should resolve within 6 months of the stress ending

questions.explanation: In ICD-11 adjustment disorder should begin within 1 months of a stressor beginning; in DSM-5 the onset should be within 3 months. Both classificatory systems indicate that the symptoms are expected to resolve within 6 months of the stressor ending. Adjustment disorder is usually managed via psychotherapeutic methods although medication can be used if necessary. It can be associated with suicidal risk that tends to resolve with the disorder. Grief can be seen as a form of adjustment disorder.

questions.question_text: Mrs Sophia Barrows is a 42-year-old woman who presents to her GP with odd skin symptoms that her GP identifies as being consistent with formication. Which of the following is true about formication?

options.text: It is strongly associated with heroin intoxication
It is a form of haptic hallucinations
It is effectively treated by SSRIs
It is not a feature of medical conditions

correct_answer.text: It is a form of haptic hallucinations

correct_answers.text: It is a form of haptic hallucinations

questions.explanation: Formication is the sensation of insects or small creatures crawling in or under the skin. It is a form of tactile or haptic hallucination. Formication is seen in stimulant intoxication (e.g. methamphetamines, cocaine) and alcohol withdrawal (i.e. delirium tremens), often with visual hallucinations of insects. Less commonly, it has been reported in benzodiazepine withdrawal, SSRI/SNRI or tramadol withdrawal and in users of opioid analgesics. Ref; Dowben JS, Kowalski PC, Keltner NL. Formication, tactile hallucinations, delusional parasitosis, and Morgellons: Enough to make your skin crawl. Perspectives in psychiatric care. 2017 Oct;53(4):220-1.

questions.question_text: In the past, transsexualism was widely understood to be defined as 'a desire to live and be accepted as a member of the opposite sex, and an accompanied discomfort of one's anatomic sex.' In our current understanding of trans, which of the following is true?

options.text: Transgender has become a much broader category
New terminology reflects personal identity rather than clinical disorder
Gender dysphoria is no longer integral
Fluidity and fluctuation in gender identity are recognised

questions.explanation: Transgender has become a much broader category. New terminology reflects a conceptual shift from clinical disorder to personal identity. Crucially, gender dysphoria is no longer integral. Fluidity and fluctuation in gender identity are recognised, with categories such as non-binary, gender-fluid, genderqueer, and pangender all recorded by clinicians at the UK's Gender Identity Development Service for under-18-year-olds. Social networking sites describe over 100 different genders, including 'agender'. Ref: Griffin L et al. Sex, gender and gender identity: a re-evaluation of the evidence. BJPsych Bulletin. 2021 Oct;45(5):291-9.

questions.question_text: Apophenia is the tendency to mistakenly perceive connections and meaning between unrelated things and was originally conceptualised as being an early symptom of schizophrenia. Who first introduced the term?
questions.explanation: Klaus Conrad coined the term apophenia in his main work, Die beginnende Schizophrenie. Versuch einer Gestaltanalyse des Wahns (1958). Ref; Mishara AL. Klaus Conrad (1905-1961): delusional mood, psychosis, and beginning schizophrenia. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2009 Dec 4:36(1):9-13.

questions.question_text: Mr Emile Jansen is a 28-year-old man who has been remanded into custody after being charged with a serious assault. The prison psychiatrist is called to see him and diagnoses Ganser syndrome. Which of the following best describes this disorder?
questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome is a rare dissociative disorder characterized by nonsensical or wrong answers to questions and other dissociative symptoms such as fugue, amnesia or conversion disorder, often with visual pseudohallucinations and a decreased state of consciousness. Psychological symptoms generally resemble the patient's sense of mental illness rather than any recognized category.

questions.question_text: Mr Roger Elliott is a 25-year-old man who is taken to the GP by his partner after he has presented with somewhat elated mood, increased activity levels and reduced sleep. He has still been attending work but has been having some more disagreements with colleagues than usual. His GP diagnoses him with a hypomanic episode. Which of the following is the length of time symptoms must be present for a diagnosis of hypomanic episode to be made?
questions.explanation: Manic symptoms must be present for one week for an episode of mania to be made, while hypomania requires 4 days of symptoms.

questions.question_text: Miss Amy Harlow is a 33-year-old woman who has a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia and struggles to take oral medication regularly. Her consultant suggests that she starts on a risperidone depot and she asks how long it will take to work. How long does risperidone depot take to reach a steady state?
questions.explanation: The long-acting, injectable formulation of risperidone usually comes in an aqueous suspension of microspheres. There is no initial drug release after injection; the main release of risperidone begins at week 2 to 3 post-injection, increases during weeks 3 and 4, is maintained during weeks 4 through 6, and declines between weeks 6 and 7. With repeated injections every 2 weeks, steady-state levels are usually reached by weeks 6 to 8. Excerpt from Knox ED, Stimmel GL. Clinical review of a long-acting, injectable formulation of risperidone. Clinical Therapeutics. 2004 Dec 1;26(12):1994-2002.

questions.question_text: Transsexualism is still classified in the ICD criteria, although this is due for revision. Which of the following is not part of the diagnostic criteria?

options.text: Desire to live as a member of the opposite sex
Wishes to be accepted as a member of the opposite sex
The individual is uncertain about their sexual orientation
The individual would want appropriate surgical intervention

correct_answer.text: The individual is uncertain about their sexual orientation

correct_answers.text: The individual is uncertain about their sexual orientation

questions.explanation: Option D is not a feature of transexualism as per ICD-10.

questions.question_text: Mr Alan Bellows is a 45 year old man who presents to his GP stating that his skin is infested with tiny insects, despite there being no objective sign of this being the case. Which of the following types of hallucinations is associated with this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: This is likely to represent delusional parasitosis, or Ekbom's syndrome, which is associated with haptic (or tactile) hallucinations that feel like insects in or on the skin. This can also be termed formication.

questions.question_text: Neurasthenia is a disorder with a wide variety of clinical manifestations, usually presenting with rapid fatigue after physical or mental effort, with other associated physical symptoms. Under which of following is neurasthenia classified in ICD 10?
questions.explanation: Neurasthenia is classified under other neurotic disorders in ICD-10.

questions.question_text: Klaus Conrad was a German neurologist and psychiatrist whose main work: 'Die beginnende Schizophrenie. Versuch einer Gestaltanalyse des Wahns' (1958), describes the early state of schizophrenia and its typical aspects. Which of the following terms describes the stage where patient finds a new psychological meaning in things around them?
questions.explanation: Apophenia is the tendency to mistakenly perceive connections and meaning between unrelated things. Klaus Conrad defined it as "unmotivated seeing of connections accompanied by a specific feeling of abnormal meaningfulness". He described the early stages of delusional thought as self-referential, over-interpretations of actual sensory perceptions, as opposed to hallucinations. Trema (stage fright) is the feeling that something very important is about to happen. Attention is drawn toward irrelevant stimuli, thoughts, and associative connections, which are distressing and unpredictable. Anastrophe is the feeling that everything revolves around the patient.

questions.question_text: Mr Edward Barnes is a 26-year-old man whose mother attends the GP, as she is worried about him. She reports that he has never been particularly interested in making friends and does not have close relationships. He has recently taken a job as a night watchman and she is worried that he is isolated. Which of the following personality disorders would he be most likely to have?
questions.explanation: This would be most likely to represent a schizoid personality disorder, wherein an individual has limited interest in making social connections or relationships with others and generally seeks out solitary occupations and interests.

questions.question_text: Mrs Georgia Dawes is a 50-year-old woman whose mother has recently died. She is very distressed and attends her GP as she wants to know how long it will take for her to recover. Which of the following is not part of normal stages of grief?
questions.explanation: The five stages of grief, as described by Elisabeth Kubler Ross and David Kessler are: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.

questions.question_text: Mr Simon Lewis is a 35-year-old man with a long-standing diagnosis of schizophrenia. He is brought to an outpatient clinic and when the doctor tries to shake hands with him, he repeatedly puts his hands out as well, but then withdraws it and eventually does not shake hands. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Ambitendency is when an individual switches between compliance and resistance to a request. They often do not eventually comply with the request. Negativism is when a patient resists requests or any attempts to move them with the same force applied. Mannerisms are repeated, seemingly goal-directed movements. Stereotypies are repetitive, non-goal-directed movements. Echopraxia is when an patient copies the movements of another person. (Ref: Walther S, et al. Structure and neural mechanisms of catatonia. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2019 Jul 1:6(7):610-9.)

questions.question_text: Chloe Timpson is a young child who is placed in Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation test. She is with her mother at the beginning but does not interact much with her. She does not seem to mind her mother leaving and does not seek her out when she returns to the room. Which type of attachment does this represent?
questions.explanation: This represents an anxious-avoidant attachment, whereby a child does not use their caregiver as a base for exploration and appears to ignore or interact little with people or objects around them. (Ref: Ainsworth MD, Bell SM. Attachment, exploration, and separation. Child development. 1970;1:49-67.).

questions.question_text: EEGs are often used to aid in the clarification and confirmation of diagnoses with different waveforms indicating particular disorders. In which of the following disorders is a 1-3Hz waveform often seen?
questions.explanation: typical absence seizures are often seen in children with learning disabilities or other seizure disorders. Onset and termination is slower than typical absence seizures and there is limited impairment of consciousness. Changes in tone are often seen. The ictal EEG shows diffuse spike waves that are slower and usually between 1.5 and 2.5 Hz. Atypical absence seizures often show slower spike-and-wave paroxysms (less than 3 Hertz) with an abnormal interictal background. (Ref: Brigo F, Striano P, Belcastro V. A reappraisal of atypical absence seizures in children and adults: therapeutic implications. Expert Opinion on Pharmacotherapy. 2019 Nov 22:20(17):2115-20.).

questions.question_text: Mrs. Helen Gower is a 76-year-old woman who has previously experienced a large stroke that resolved two years ago. She developed vascular dementia following this stroke. What is the most likely neurological deficit that can be seen now?
questions.explanation: There are no typical focal neurological signs associated with vascular cognitive impairment. In the presence of large-territory infarcts focal signs such as hemiparesis and circumduction gait may be apparent. In those with the more common small vessel diseases, milder gait disturbances and parkinsonism, dysarthria, dysphagia, rigidity, and hypokinesia and as well to hemimotor dysfunction is seen. On average, reflex asymmetry was the most prevalent symptom (49% in one series) in vascular dementia. (Ref: Graff-Radford J. Vascular cognitive impairment. Continuum: Lifelong Learning in Neurology. 2019 Feb;25(1):147)

questions.question_text: Mrs Alice Moor is a 72-year-old woman who has experienced a CVA. She is unable to copy intersecting pentagons. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: This is Constructional apraxia whereby an individual is unable to draw or copy shapes or patterns. Ideational apraxia is when an individual loses the ability to plan movements related to using objects. Ideomotor apraxia is when an individual struggles to imitate or mime movements, such as brushing their hair or teeth. Oculomotor apraxia describes an individual being unable to move their eyes voluntarily; it is seen in Balint's syndrome. Limb-kinetic apraxia is an impairment of co-ordinating voluntary movements of limbs.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a listed form of schizophrenia in the ICD-10 or DSM-5?
questions.explanation: ICD-10 includes various schizophrenia subtypes, including paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, simple, residual and undifferentiated. DSM-IV included subtypes but these were removed entirely in DSM-5. Disorganised schizophrenia was in DSM-IV and was the equivalent to hebephrenia. (Ref: Mattila T et al. Impact of DSM-5 changes on the diagnosis and acute treatment of schizophrenia. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2015;41(3):637-643).

questions.question_text: Screening tools can be useful in terms of identifying individuals who may be at high risk of having a mental health disorder. They are not generally considered to be diagnostic. Which of the following is a screening tool?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, PHQ-9 and AUDIT are examples of screening tools. Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS), Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS), Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), Hamilton depression rating scale, and Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale measure the severity of given conditions. (Ref: Cox JL, Holden JM and Sagovsky R. Detection of Postnatal Depression: Development of the 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. British Journal of Psychiatry; 1987; 150, 782-786).

questions.question_text: The trail-making test is used in the assessment of patients with suspected cognitive impairment. Which of the following cognitive functions does it assess?
questions.explanation: The trail-making test is used to assess processing speed and executive functioning. The first part of the test involves the patient having to 'join the dots' with a sequence of numbers and this assesses processing speed. The second part is similar but alternates between numbers and letters and this assesses executive functioning in terms of set-shifting.

questions.question_text: Daniel Barker is a child who has recently received an EEG to clarify his diagnosis. He is identified as having 'hypsarrhythmia'. What is his likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypsarrhythmia is a very chaotic EEG with no discernable pattern. It is associated with infantile spasms, a form of epilepsy that occurs in infants that can have a poor prognosis, depending upon the likely causative factors. The most common clinical description is a sudden, symmetric, tonic muscle contraction producing flexion/extension of the trunk and extremities, although a variety of movement patterns have been described. (Ref: Demarest ST, et al. The impact of hypsarrhythmia on infantile spasms treatment response: observational cohort study from the National Infantile Spasms Consortium. Epilepsia. 2017 Dec;58(12):2098-103).

questions.question_text: The Eysenck Personality Questionnaire is designed to measure the personality traits of an individual. Which of the following is true of this questionnaire?

options.text: It measures only extraversion/introversion and neuroticism/stability
Introversion is thought to associate with increased activity in the reticular activating system
It is not useful across different cultures
High neuroticism is thought to be associated with impulsive behaviour

correct_answer.text: Introversion is thought to associate with increased activity in the reticular activating system

correct_answers.text: Introversion is thought to associate with increased activity in the reticular activating system

questions.explanation: Eysenck's Personality Questionnaire incorporates scales measuring extraversion/introversion, neuroticism/stability and psychoticism/socialization, as well as incorporating a lie scale. It has been found to be applicable across various cultures. Eysenck theorised that introverts had greater activity in the reticular activating system and so found additional stimuli overwhelming, leading to introverted behaviour. Conversely, extraverts has less activity and so seek out stimuli. (Ref: Bullock WA and Gilliland K. Eysenck's arousal theory of introversion-extraversion: A converging measures investigation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology; 1993; 64 (1): 113-123).

questions.question_text: Among psychiatric inpatients, which of the following is the most common sign of catatonia reported?
questions.explanation: Catatonia is often rated for clinical and research purposes using Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS). When BFCRS is used among psychiatric inpatients, the most common catatonic features observed includes mutism, immobility, staring, withdrawal, posturing and negativism. These features were all noted in at least 50% of a prospectively identified consecutive series of hospital admissions (Ref: Mormando & Francis (2020) Catatonia revived: a unique syndrome updated. International Review of Psychiatry, 32:5-6, 403-411)

questions.question_text: Mr Henry Waterhouse is a 28 year old junior barrister who has been referred to his occupational health department due to concerns around his behaviour. He has been noted to make derogatory comments about more senior staff, stating that he is more able than them and should be promoted immediately. They suspect that he has undermined the work of other members of staff to embarrass them and promote his own results. When confronted with these suspicions, he is outraged, dismisses them and shows no awareness of why they may have arisen. Which of the following personality disorders is he most likely to meet the criteria for?
questions.explanation: This is most likely to represent narcissistic personality disorder which is characterised by an inflated sense of self-importance, need for recognition or praise and a lack of empathy for others. Individuals are often preoccupied by thoughts or plans to gain greater influence or power and may take advantage of others to achieve these ends.

questions.question_text: Mrs Belinda Bosco is a 36 year old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. During his most recent episode he was lying on his bed immobile much of the time. After recovering he described very vivid experiences and states that he felt like he was flying through space. Which of the following best describes this scenario?
questions.explanation: An oneiroid state is when an individual experiences extremely vivid and all-encompassing hallucinations, often, but not invariably, associated with catatonic symptoms.

questions.question_text: Mark Coombes is a 78-year-old man who has been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy Bodies following a period of variable cognitive impairment, falls and intermittent visual hallucinations. He has recently received a scan and his children want to know about the result. Which of the following are true regarding imaging findings in Dementia with Lewy Bodies?

options.text: Pathological nigrostriatal uptake on DAT scan
DAT scans can distinguish it from Parkinson's disease
More pronounced posterior parietal grey matter loss than in Alzheimer's disease
It preferentially affects frontotemporal white matter tracts
There is more diffuse cerebral atrophy than in Alzheimer's disease

correct_answer.text: Pathological nigrostriatal uptake on DAT scan

correct_answers.text: Pathological nigrostriatal uptake on DAT scan

questions.explanation: Dementia with Lewy Bodies is associated with profoundly reduced radiotracer uptake in the substantia nigra and striatal region on DAT scans. This is also found in Parkinson's disease, although there is less generalised grey matter loss in the latter condition. Dementia with Lewy Bodies tends to show less diffuse cerebral atrophy and grey matter loss than Alzheimer's disease. The medial temporal lobe and entorhinal cortex tends to be preserved. Neuromelanin MRI shows decreased hyperintensity in the lateral part of the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus indicating dopamine neuronal loss. In perfusion SPECT, a bilateral occipital hypoperfusion is frequently observed in DLB. Outside the brian, markedly decreased uptake of MIBG-1231-metaiodobenzylguanidine on myocardial scintigraphy is also observed in DLB.. (Ref: Yousaf T, Dervenoulas G, Valkimadi PE and Politis M. Neuroimaging in Lewy body dementia. Journal of Neurology; 2019 Jan;266(1):1-26).

questions.question_text: Mr Phillip Conrad is a 42-year-old man who is currently receiving psychodynamic psychotherapy following experiencing significant abuse in early childhood. His mother supports him in the community and there are independent records that indicate she was involved in the abuse and that he was aware of this. However, he insists he has no memory of this. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: This is most likely to represent retrospective falsification, which refers to a psychological concept whereby an individual unconsciously 'forgets' or distorts past memories to better meet their current needs. It would be emotionally threatening for the patient to recall their mother's involvement in their abuse and so the memories are unconsciously repressed.

questions.question_text: EEGs are often used to aid in the clarification and confirmation of diagnoses with different waveforms indicating particular disorders. In which of the following is a waveform of 3-6Hz seen?
questions.explanation: Typical absence seizures are characterised by brief and abrupt impairment of consciousness, with the patient ceasing whatever activity they were engaged in and then restarting it once the episode ends, usually without any awareness of what has occurred. During seizure activity, the EEG shows a characteristic regular and symmetrical generalised discharges of 3-4?Hz "spike and slow" wave complexes, and may also have multiple spike and slow wave complexes. The interictal EEG tends to be normal. (Ref: Panayiotopoulos CP. Typical absence seizures and their treatment. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 1999;81:351-355).

questions.question_text: Mr. Bill Watkins is a 56-year-old man who is taking part in a research study as a healthy control subject. He reports, "I can see the places I've visited vividly, I can bring it up at will, and it lingers in my memory". What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: This describes eidetic memory wherein an individual can vividly recall images from their memory in great detail, even after having had limited exposure to them.

questions.question_text: Daniel Givens is a 5-year-old boy who does not want to eat his vegetables at dinner. However, he eats them if his parents allow him a dessert whenever he eats vegetables. Over time, he starts to reliably eat the vegetables on his plate. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Premack's principle suggests that if a person wants to perform a given activity, the person will perform a less desirable activity to get at the more desirable activity; that is, activities may themselves be reinforcers. An individual will be more motivated to perform a particular activity if he knows that he will partake in a more desirable activity as a consequence. It is an important concept in applied behaviour analysis.

questions.question_text: According to the James-Lange Theory what is the cause of emotions?
questions.explanation: The James-Lange theory is a hypothesis on the origin and nature of emotions and is one of the earliest theories of emotion within modern psychology. Two 19th-century scholars, William James and Carl Lange, developed it independently. The premise of the theory is that physiological arousal instigates the experience of emotions.

questions.question_text: Mr. John Peppers is an office manager who is interviewing a potential new employee. Before the interview he discovers that the interviewee recently received a speeding fine and immediately rules them out for the job and thinks of the person as wholly bad. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: The halo effect is the tendency for a person's positive or negative traits to "spill over" from one personality area to another in others' perceptions of them. Fundamental attribution erroг is the tendency for people to over-emphasise personality-based explanations for behaviours observed in others while under-emphasising the role and power of situational influences on the same behaviour. Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy to the opinion of an authority figure (unrelated to its content) and be more influenced by that opinion. Ingroup bias is the tendency to give preferential treatment to others perceived to be members of one's own group. Group attribution error is the biased belief that the characteristics of an individual group member are reflective of the group as a whole or the tendency to assume that group decision outcomes reflect the preferences of group members, even when information is available that clearly suggests otherwise.

questions.question_text: A manager wishes to assess the efficiency of a mental health team in terms of their administrative tasks. They note that they show a higher efficiency when the manager is actively observing but lower at other times. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect (also referred to as the observer effect) is a type of psychological reactivity in which individuals modify an aspect of their behavior in response to their awareness of being observed. The subject-expectancy effect is a form of reactivity that occurs in scientific experiments or medical treatments when a research subject or patient expects a given result and therefore unconsciously affects the outcome, or reports the expected result. The observer-expectancy effect is when a researcher's cognitive bias causes them to subconsciously influence the participants of an experiment. These are both managed via double-blind methodology. The novelty effect, in the context of human performance, is the tendency for performance to initially improve when new technology is instituted, not because of any actual improvement in learning or achievement, but in response to increased interest in the new technology. The John Henry effect is an experimental bias introduced into social experiments by the reactive behaviour of the control group. In a controlled social experiment, if a control is aware of their status as members of the control group and is able to compare their performance with that of the treatment group, members of the control group may actively work harder to overcome the "disadvantage" of being in the control group.

questions.question_text: Prejudice is defined as an affective feeling towards a person or group member based solely on that person's group membership. It is a word that is often used to refer to preconceived, usually unfavourable, feelings towards people or a person because of their personal characteristics. Which of the following is most likely to decrease prejudice?

options.text: Learning more about the other group
Reducing unplanned contact with the other group

correct_answer.text: Learning more about the other group

correct_answers.text: Learning more about the other group

questions.explanation: Learning more about other groups, particularly via regular direct contact, has been shown to diminish prejudice. Diversity training in the workplace and similar does not have a robust evidence base.

questions.question_text: Mr. Edvard Munch is an 82-year-old man who is being investigated for possible cognitive impairment. In the course of his assessment he is asked to read a list of words and, after 10 minutes, to repeat them. What form of memory does this test?
questions.explanation: This would be best described as a test of long-term memory as short-term memories tend to degrade within seconds.

questions.question_text: Procedural memory is a type of implicit memory, which aids the performance of particular types of tasks. Which area of the brain is associated with it?
questions.explanation: Procedural memory is thought to relate to the basal ganglia, cerebellum and limbic system.

questions.question_text: In which of the following psychotherapeutic approaches, the patient is asked to sit facing an empty chair?
questions.explanation: Fritz Perls formulated the Gestalt therapy that aims to consider the individual as a whole that is connected to his/her environment and social milieu. The patient is asked to address an empty chair, picturing a person with whom they are experiencing conflict. The patient is encouraged to explain his/her feelings and understanding of the conflict. Ref: Lysiak M. Dialogical temporal chair technique. British Journal of Guidance & Counselling. 2017 Dec 9:1-9.

questions.question_text: There are various theories around the development, storage and loss of memories. Which of the following best describes Ribot's law of retrograde amnesia?

options.text: Childhood memories tend to be inaccurate
Memories are affected by an individual's mood at the time
More recent memories are more likely to be lost
Certain sensory inputs improve memory recall

correct_answer.text: More recent memories are more likely to be lost

correct_answers.text: More recent memories are more likely to be lost

questions.explanation: An intriguing aspect of retrograde amnesia is its temporal gradient. The memories most vulnerable to disruption are those that were formed in the more recent past, compared to older memories. This relationship is known as Ribot's Law after the French neurologist who first documented it. Ref; Parkin AJ. Human memory: the hippocampus is the key. Current Biology. 1996 Dec 1;6(12):1583-5.

questions.question_text: Working memory is a cognitive system with a limited capacity that is responsible for temporarily holding information available for processing. Which of the following best describes the number of items that most people can hold in their working memory?
questions.explanation: Most adults can repeat about seven digits in correct order. Ref: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63, 81-97.

questions.question_text: Fundamental attribution error is a cognitive bias that was coined by Lee Ross some years after a classic experiment by Edward E. Jones and Victor Harris. Which of the following is true of fundamental attribution error?

options.text: It is more common in Western societies
It is judging yourself according to situation
It is focusing on a specific element of a situation
It is believing that what people think is who they are
It is judging others in context

correct_answer.text: It is more common in Western societies

correct_answers.text: It is more common in Western societies

questions.explanation: Fundamental attribution error is the tendency for people to under-emphasize situational explanations for another individual's observed behaviour while over-emphasizing dispositional and personality-based explanations for their own behaviour. It tends to be more common in the West and less so in more collectivist societies.

questions.question_text: Miss Zoe Falstaff is a 20-year-old woman with a profound fear of snakes. Which of the following is this most likely to be an example of?
questions.explanation: In psychology, stimulus preparedness is a concept developed to explain why certain associations are learned more readily than others. For example, phobias related to survival, such as snakes, spiders, and heights, are much more common and much easier to induce in the laboratory than other kinds of fears.

questions.question_text: Hypnotic suggestibility describes how likely a given individual is to respond positively to hypnosis and hypnotic suggestion. Which of the following is true of high hypnotic suggestibility?

options.text: Necessary for hypnosis to be effective

questions.explanation: Metacognitive agency refers to an individual's ability to monitor his or her own ability to influence the world. There is evidence to suggest that reduced metacognitive agency, i.e. a less robust awareness of how effective an individual is at affecting the world, may be associated with increased suggestibility with regards to hypnosis. (Ref: Devin B. Terhune DB and Hedmana LRA. Metacognition of agency is reduced in high hypnotic suggestibility. Cognition; 2017 November; 168: 176-181).

questions.question_text: Dan Sokel is a 5-year-old boy who has developed a profound fear of going to the park after being knocked over by a Labrador there and vigorously licked, which he found very upsetting. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: This represents classical or Pavlovian conditioning which is when a potent stimulus is associated with a previously neutral stimulus until learning occurs. This can require repeated exposures, but can take only one if it is sufficiently potent. Pavlov first demonstrated it using dogs. In this situation, the boy has learnt a phobia of going to the park after it was associated with a single aversive experience.

questions.question_text: Peter Holmes is a 6-year-old boy who is pestering his parents for sweets while they are on a shopping trip. His parents tell him that he can have one sweet now if he wants but that if he waits until they are home, then he can have an ice-lolly, which they know he would prefer. He chooses to wait and not ask for sweets any longer. Which of the following best describes the above scenario?
questions.explanation: This scenario describes an example of delayed gratification. This is when an individual, such as the boy in the example, foregoes an immediate reward in favour of a later, and often greater, reward at a later point. It was well demonstrated by Walter Mischel in his marshmallow experiments with 4 year olds. They were advised that they could have one marshmallow now or two if they waited 15 minutes. Those who were able to wait tended to have greater academic success, self-worth and ability to cope with stress, and a lower likelihood of exhibiting unhelpful behaviours. (Ref: Mischel W, Shoda Y, Rodriguez MI. Delay of gratification in children. Science. 1989 May 26;244(4907):933-8.).

questions.question_text: Learned helplessness is a concept in behavioural psychology. Which of the following is true regarding this concept?

options.text: It is associated with reduced levels of serotonin in the raphe nucleus
It was first demonstrated in animal models
It is thought to be linked to the development of psychotic disorders
It is associated with positive cognitive styles

correct_answer.text: It was first demonstrated in animal models

correct_answers.text: It was first demonstrated in animal models

questions.explanation: Learned helplessness is a behaviour seen when individuals are repeatedly exposed to aversive stimuli and cannot escape them. They then cease to try to avoid them, even if presented with the possibility of doing so. Seligman first demonstrated it with dogs. It is associated with negative cognitive styles and depression related difficulties. It has not been specifically linked to psychosis. Subjects thought to demonstrate learned helplessness have elevated levels of serotonin in the raphe nucleus. (Ref: Maier SF, Seligman ME. Learned helplessness at fifty: Insights from neuroscience. Psychological review. 2016 Jul; 123(4):349.

questions.question_text: Which of the following processes increases the likelihood that a minority group can influence decision-making?

options.text: Minority group seen as different to majority
Lack of dissent among the majority

questions.explanation: Minority groups are more likely to be able to influence majority groups if their views are expressed consistently, flexibly and in a manner that is appealing to the majority. Being similar to the majority is also helpful, as is not having a very small minority group, which can be dismissed as an outlier. (Ref: Butera F, Falomir-Pichastor JM, Mugny G, Quiamzade A. Minority influence. The Oxford handbook of social influence. 2017 Jul 7:317-37).

questions.question_text: Charlotte Tomkins is a 4-year-old girl who has had some difficulty learning to be dry at night and is still experiencing some nocturnal enuresis. Her parents use a star chart to reward her for nights when she remains dry with positive results. Which of the following best describes this?
questions.explanation: This is a demonstration of operant conditioning in which a behaviour is encouraged or discouraged via explicit reinforcement, e.g. via a star chart, or punishment. Skinner first demonstrated this via experiments with pigeons and rats in the Skinner box.

questions.question_text: Which of the following behavioural treatments in sexual deviancy is an aversion technique?
questions.explanation: Shame aversion therapy is a contentious technique for the treatment of persons practicing deviant sexual acts such as transvestism, voyeurism, pedophilia, exhibitionism and frotteurism. It consists of having the subject who is embarrassed or self-conscious about the act he performs perform the act on demand in front of a number of observers. The act is made to continue for 15 to 35 min and its style kept as close to the in vivo situation as is possible. The patient is told simply to observe himself and be aware of being observed. (Serber M. Shame aversion therapy. Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry. 1970 Sep 1;1(3):213-5.)

questions.question_text: Mrs. Anne Walters is working as a nurse in an acute admissions unit. She is being observed as part of an audit of staff activity and finds that she gets more done during the day than usual. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Zajonc's in 1965 described the drive theory of social facilitation, according to which the mere presence of others increases arousal, facilitating the frequency of responses with the greatest habit strength (dominant responses). More broadly, social facilitation is said to occur "when one animal increases or decreases its behavior in the presence of another animal which does not otherwise interact with it". Conformity describes matching one's attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors to those of a given group, often the dominant one in the society. Social normalization is the process through which beliefs or activities that are considered unusual gradually become considered as "normal". Groupthink occurs when a desire for harmony within a group leads to dysfunctional decision-making, often leading to undesirable outcomes. Socialisation describes how an individual comes to learn and accept the norms of their society. Ref: Brown AJ, Harkins SG. Social Facilitation and Social Loafing: Opposite Sides of the Same Coin. InIndividual Motivation within Groups 2020 Jan 1 (pp. 297-330). Academic Press.

questions.question_text: The Q sort test is used in psychology and social sciences. Which of the following does it measure?
questions.explanation: Q methodology uses a form of factor analysis to find correlations between variables across a number of subjects. It is used in research to understand how people think about an issue (subjective viewpoints), and in clinical practice to assess patients. It often uses the method of individuals, either patients or clinicians, ordering statements about a condition or patient in order of relevance. (Ref: Block, J. The Q-sort method in personality assessment and psychiatric research. Springfield, IL: C. C. Thomas; reprinted 1978, Palo Alto, CA: Consulting Psychology Press).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best describes the concept of group polarisation?

options.text: The tendency of a group to favour its own members over others
The tendency for a group to make a more extreme decision than its individual members would have done initially
The tendency of a group to select individuals to blame for adverse outcomes
The tendency for a group to engage in irrational decision-making to preserve harmony
Individuals losing self-awareness while in a group setting

correct_answer.text: The tendency for a group to make a more extreme decision than its individual members would have done initially

correct_answers.text: The tendency for a group to make a more extreme decision than its individual members would have done initially

questions.explanation: Group polarisation is defined within social psychology as the tendency for groups to move towards a more extreme version of their initial beliefs following group discussion, e.g. being more risky if they were originally inclined to be, and more cautious if this was their initial inclination. (Ref: Arvan, M. 2019. 'The Dark Side of Morality: Group Polarization and Moral Epistemology'. Philosophical Forum 50:87-115).

questions.question_text: Social stigma, also called public stigma, refers to negative stereotypes of those with a mental health problem. Which of the following is true regarding stigmatisation in England?

options.text: Increased mental health knowledge is associated with increased stigma.
People being open about their mental health increase the risk of stigmatisation.
The idea that people can pull them together decrease stigmatisation.
People with mental health difficulties are seen as difficult to talk to.
People with mental health difficulties are not viewed as dangerous.

correct_answer.text: People with mental health difficulties are seen as difficult to talk to.

correct_answers.text: People with mental health difficulties are seen as difficult to talk to.

questions.explanation: Stigma around mental health disorders is common, even among those who have regular contact with people with mental health difficulties. Increased knowledge is associated with reduced stigma. Schizophrenia and alcohol and substance misuse disorders are associated with perceptions of dangerousness, with the latter also being seen as self-inflicted, with this increasing the sense of stigmatisation. People with mental health difficulties are perceived as being difficult to talk to. Greater openness and discussion of mental health in the public sphere may be associated with more positive perceptions. Ref: Mehta N et al. Public attitudes towards people with mental illness in England and Scotland, 1994-2003. Br J Psychiatry. 2009;194(3):278-284.

questions.question_text: Mr Arthur Bradley is a 68-year-old man who has been diagnosed with gastric carcinoma. He has the option of intervention but, after discussing the likelihood of success with the medical team, decides he would not want to have it. The multidisciplinary team respects his decision and he dies after receiving appropriate palliative care. Which of the following ethical principles has been applied here?
questions.explanation: This is an example of autonomy, the right of competent adults to make informed decisions about their own medical care. The principle underlies the requirement to seek the consent or informed agreement of the patient before any investigation or treatment takes place.

questions.question_text: Mr Wayne Hevers is a 36-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has been trialled on Clozapine but unfortunately developed agranulocytosis. He recovered but continued to have significant psychotic symptoms. His consultant explored the idea of a re-challenge with Clozapine but, after finding that there was no example of this being successfully done after agranulocytosis, elected not to try Clozapine again and explore other treatment options. Which of the following ethical principles has been applied here?
questions.explanation: The concept of non-maleficence is embodied by the phrase, "first, do no harm". It is avoiding doing unnecessary harm to a patient. It must necessarily be balanced against beneficence, or doing good for the patient, as most treatments have potential side-effects. However, when delivering a treatment, a practitioner should proceed on the basis that it is likely that the treatment will do more good than harm. A treatment, which caused marked harm for little or limited benefit would not be acceptable.

questions.question_text: Holmes and Rahe were psychiatrists who proposed a scale and rating system of life events by how stressful they would be and suggested that if an individual experienced a given amount of a stress, that their likelihood of becoming mentally unwell would increase. Which of the following did they rate as the most stressful life event?
questions.explanation: eath of a spouse was rated most highly, with divorce and separation from partner following it. (Ref: Holmes TH, Rahe RH (1967). The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research; 11(2): 213-8).

questions.question_text: The ÆSOP study was a multicentre case control study intended to investigate psychosis in the UK. Which of the following factors was observed by the ÆSOP study to be associated with a 9-fold increase in the risk of schizophrenia amongst immigrants?
questions.explanation: The ÆSOP study was meant to investigate the increased rate of psychosis amongst African-Caribbean populations in the UK. It identified that immigrants of Afro-Caribbean origin were 9 times more likely to develop schizophrenia than the general population. (Ref: Morgan C, et al. Ethnicity and long-term course and outcome of psychotic disorders in a UK sample: the ÆSOP-10 study. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2017 Aug 211(2):88-94).

questions.question_text: Much research has focused upon risk factors for schizophrenia, including those related to an individual's surroundings or circumstances. Which of the following has been best established as increasing the risk of developing schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: It has been consistently found that migrants and their children have an increased risk of developing schizophrenia compared to the general population. Social deprivation has been linked to schizophrenia but it is also associated with a variety of other adverse factors, which may also contribute to the illness. (Ref: Selten JP, van der Ven E, Termorshuizen F. Migration and psychosis: a meta-analysis of incidence studies. Psychological medicine. 2020 Jan 50(2):303-13).

questions.question_text: Miss Joanna Temple is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder. She has a history of medication non-compliance and was previously given lithium carbonate but took more than her prescribed dose and developed toxicity. She continues to be unreliable with medication. She has attended her outpatient clinic and asked to trial lithium again but her psychiatrist has advised against this. Which of the following principles is relevant to this scenario?
questions.explanation: Non-maleficence is the concept of "primum non nocere" or first, do no harm. It refers to the obligation to not take actions or give advice which is likely to cause more harm to the patient than benefit. In this scenario, while Lithium is an entirely reasonable treatment, it is unlikely that the patient will take it in a safe and effective manner and so the risk of harm is greater than the likelihood of benefit.

questions.question_text: In Kohlberg's theory of gender development, a child realises that their gender is not dependant on the way they act or how others treat them. This is called
questions.explanation: Kohlberg emphasised cognition as occurring before action and behaviour. He described 3 stages of children understanding their gender identity and role. 1) Gender identity - The child identifies as male or female and can label others as well. 2) Gender stability - The identity in which they recognise themselves as does not change. 3) Gender consistency - The acceptance that gender does not change, regardless of changes in gender-typed appearance, activities and traits.

questions.question_text: Which of the following life events is the most stressful for people living in Western countries?

options.text: Death of a close family member

correct_answer.text: Death of a close family member

correct_answers.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation: Holmes and Rahe developed a questionnaire called the Social Readjustment Rating Scale for identifying major stressful life events. They rated death of a spouse as the most stressful event, followed by divorce and marital separation. Of the above, death of a close family member is the highest rated, just below incarceration and above major personal injury or illness.

questions.question_text: Attachment style in infants is tested using several variants of the Strange Situation Test developed by Margaret Ainsworth. Which of the following kinds of attachment describe the scenario wherein the child shows little reaction when the mother leaves the room but acts frozen upon her return?
questions.explanation: This best describes a disorganised attachment whereby an infant is unsure of the behaviour of the mother and shows reactions that either do not clearly correlate with the presence or absence of a caregiver or where they show signs of stress without necessarily approaching or ignoring the parent. Securely attached children tend to be distressed when the caregiver leaves but reassured on their return. Insecure attachments come in two forms, the avoidant where the child reacts little to the presence or absence of the parent, and ambivalent where they are clingy before separation and difficult to comfort.

questions.question_text: Certain fears are recognised as beginning at certain ages in children and can be viewed as appropriate for their stage of development. At what age is fear of loud noises most prominent?
questions.explanation: Very young children, from birth onwards, can be startled by sudden, loud noises. This continues from the age of one year onwards.

questions.question_text: Certain fears are recognised as beginning at certain ages in children and can be viewed as appropriate for their stage of development. At what age does the fear of death become apparent?
questions.explanation: Fear of death usually starts after the age of 7, as conceptualising it as a concept requires a certain degree of abstract thought.

questions.question_text: In which of the following stages of child development does 'conservation' occur?
questions.explanation: Conservation refers to a logical thinking ability that allows a person to determine that a certain quantity will remain the same despite adjustment of the container, shape, or apparent size,. According to developmental psychologist Jean Piaget, conservation becomes apparent in the concrete operational stage between the ages of 7-11 years.

questions.question_text: At which of the following Freudian stages of development girls understand their gender and said to experience envy of their mothers?
questions.explanation: The phallic stage of Freud's psychosexual development theory corresponds with the Electra Complex, in which a girl competes with her mother for possession of her father.

questions.question_text: Pregnancy is a period of significant change and can be associated with a greater burden of mental health disorders. Which of the following does pregnancy appear to be protective against?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is associated with a low rate of suicide, despite the higher burden of mental disorders. (Ref: Whitlock FA and Edwards JE. Pregnancy and attempted suicide. Comprehensive Psychiatry; 1968 Jan; 9(1): 1-12. Marzuk PM, Tardiff K, Leon AC, Hirsch CS, Portera L, Hartwell N, and Iqbal MI. The American Journal of Psychiatry 1997 Jan 1, 154(1):122-123).

questions.question_text: Privation has a specific definition within the field of developmental psychology. Which of the following best defines privation?

options.text: A child being exposed to persistent poverty and the consequences of this
A child having no opportunity to have a relationship with a caregiver
A child having a relationship with a physically abusive caregiver
A child not having educational opportunities
A child having a relationship with a caregiver severed

correct_answer.text: A child having no opportunity to have a relationship with a caregiver

correct_answers.text: A child having no opportunity to have a relationship with a caregiver

questions.explanation: In psychology, privation occurs when a child has no opportunity to form a relationship with a parental figure. It is different to deprivation, which occurs when an established relationship is severed. It is understood that privation can produce social, emotional and intellectual problems for children. Ref; O'Connor TG, et al. The effects of global severe privation on cognitive competence: Extension and longitudinal follow-up. Child development. 2000 Mar;71(2):376-90.

questions.question_text: A group is called upon to make a decision and, following discussion, the group's initial idea is strengthened. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Group polarisation refers to the tendency for a group to make decisions that are more extreme than the initial inclination of its members. These more extreme decisions are towards greater risk if individuals' initial tendencies are to be risky and towards greater caution if individuals' initial tendencies are to be cautious. Groupthink is a psychological phenomenon that occurs within a group of people in which the desire for harmony or conformity in the group results in an irrational or dysfunctional decision-making outcome. Group members try to minimize conflict and reach a consensus decision without critical evaluation of alternative viewpoints by actively suppressing dissenting viewpoints, and by isolating themselves from outside influences. In-group bias is a pattern of favoring members of one's in-group over out-group members. Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs or hypotheses. Herd behaviour is the behaviour of individuals in a group acting collectively without centralized direction.

questions.question_text: Homeostasis refers to the bodily mechanisms that maintain a steady internal state. Which of the following aspects of human biology best demonstrates the existence of physiological homeostasis?
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the state of steady internal conditions maintained by living things and is a dynamic state of equilibrium that is the condition of optimal functioning for the organism and includes many variables, such as body temperature and fluid balance, being kept within certain pre-set limits (homeostatic range). Homeostasis confers a natural resistance to perturbations in the optimal conditions.

questions.question_text: Sam Parker is an 8-year-old boy who has had difficulty socialising and making eye contact throughout his childhood. He has been referred to a Child and Adolescent Mental Health service for an assessment. Which of the following brain areas is most likely to exhibit a structural abnormality?
questions.explanation: ASD has been associated with abnormalities in the cerebellar vermis more often that in the other brain regions listed. Ref: Wang SS, Kloth AD, Badura A. The cerebellum, sensitive periods, and autism. Neuron. 2014 Aug 6;83(3):518-32.

questions.question_text: Intellectual disability is categorised via the IQ level of the individual rather than by measures of function or symptoms. Which of the following IQ ranges is indicative of moderate intellectual disability?
questions.explanation: The ranges for intellectual disability are Profound <20, Severe - 20-34, Moderate - 35-49, Mild-50-70 and Borderline - 71-85

questions.question_text: Peter Chatterley is a 7-year-old boy who tends to leave his toys scattered around the house after he plays with them. His mother brings in a star chart to encourage him to tidy up after himself and this works over a period of a few weeks. Which of the following best describes this approach?
questions.explanation: Operant conditioning is a learning process through which the strength of a behaviour is modified by reinforcement or punishment. Classical conditioning refers to a learning procedure in which a biologically potent stimulus (e.g. food) is paired with a previously neutral stimulus (e.g. a bell). It also refers to the learning process that results from this pairing, through which the neutral stimulus comes to elicit a response that is similar to the one elicited by the potent stimulus.

questions.question_text: The Camberwell Family Interview was developed in 1972 by Brown, Birley and Wing. Which of the following does it assess?

options.text: Assessing motivation to discontinue alcohol misuse

questions.explanation: The Camberwell Family Interview was designed to identify high expressed emotions in family members of patients with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Margaret Mahler developed the separation-individuation theory of child development, which divided it into various stages. At which of the following stages is a 1-week-old baby?
questions.explanation: Margaret Mahler's theory: Normal autistic phase - First few weeks of life. The infant is detached and self-absorbed. Spends most of his/her time sleeping. Mahler later abandoned this phase, based on new findings from her infant research believing it to be non-existent. The phase still appears in many books on her theories.

questions.question_text: By the age of 4, most children will have an awareness of their gender and that of others, as well as ideas about what this may mean. Which of the following forms of learning drives this process?
questions.explanation: According to Social Learning Theory individuals develop gender concept by imitating role models. This takes place through observational learning and vicarious reinforcements from caregivers. (Ref: Fagot BI, Leinbach MD. Gender identity: some thoughts on an old concept. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. 1985 Nov).

questions.question_text: Lev Vygotsky was a psychologist who developed various theories around human development . Which of the following best describes the theories he developed?
questions.explanation: Lev Vygotsky developed theories around the zone of proximal development and how culture influences cognitive development, sometimes termed cultural-historical psychology. Ref: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.01515/full

questions.question_text: Peter Atters is a 6-year-old boy whose parents are trying to get him to tidy his room before bedtime. They decide to use a STAR chart to encourage him. Which of the following terms describes using the process of sticking stars on a chart to modify behaviour?
questions.explanation: This is an example of operant conditioning, which is a learning process through which the strength of behaviour is modified by reinforcement or punishment.

questions.question_text: Psychologists such as Skinner used animals to develop theories around human behaviour. Rhesus monkeys were used in a seminal study around which of the following phenomena?
questions.explanation: Harry Harlow used rhesus monkeys to demonstrate the importance of contact comfort to infants in terms of attachment theory. Infant rhesus monkeys were placed in isolation with their terry cloth or wire mesh "mothers", one of whom had a milk bottle. The infants invariably preferred the cloth "mothers" even when they could not provide milk.

questions.question_text: Holmes and Rahe were psychiatrists who developed a stress scale of 43 life events that can contribute to illness by reviewing the notes of 5000 patients. Which of the following is the life event with the biggest impact according to their stress scale?
questions.explanation: Death of a spouse was rated as the life event with the greatest impact, with this being followed by divorce, marital separation, imprisonment, death of a close family member and personal illness or injury.

questions.question_text: Mr Oliver Stemp is a 16-year-old boy who is currently feeling uncertain about his sexual orientation. Which of the following stages of development could this represent?
questions.explanation: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development are a psychoanalytic theory that identifies a series of eight stages that a healthy developing individual should pass through from infancy to late adulthood. The adolescent stage of role confusion vs. identity is usually described as the time when an individual develops a sense of sexual identity.

questions.question_text: As individuals age, changes occur within the structure of the brain. Which of the following is considered an expected pattern of structural brain change occurring in adolescence?

options.text: Increase in white matter and decrease in grey matter
Decrease in grey and white matter
Increase in grey matter and decrease in white matter
Increase in white matter and no change in grey matter
Increase in grey and white matter

correct_answer.text: Increase in white matter and decrease in grey matter

correct_answers.text: Increase in white matter and decrease in grey matter

questions.explanation: It appears that adolescents undergo a gradual increase in white matter volume, particularly in the corpus callosum and prefrontal cortex, and a decrease in grey matter volume, although there is evidence that the density of the remaining grey matter increases. Some of the recent studies suggest that the apparent grey matter reduction is likely to be due to both pruning of dendrites as well as increased intracortical myelination (Ref: Patel Y, et al. Cerebral Cortex. 2018 Aug 28;29(8):3351-62).

questions.question_text: Sophia Evans is a 3-day-old baby. Her parents are worried that she does not seem to be able to see them clearly but are reassured when the medical team explain the development of vision in infants. Which of the following visual abilities is normally present in newborns?
questions.explanation: At birth, newborns can see around 8-10 inches and have pupillary reflexes. They can track objects within a few months and focus on a nearby face by 8 weeks. Depth perception and colour vision are generally not present until 5 months of age. Accommodation develops around 3-4 months of age.

questions.question_text: Mr Aman Khan is a 30-year-old man who is in a stable relationship with his partner and holding down a secure job. His partner has recently brought up plans to live together. Which of the following stages of development is he likely to be going through?
questions.explanation: Erikson theorised that between the ages of 20-40 years of age, the main development stage is intimacy vs. isolation and defined by the existential question "Can I love?".

questions.question_text: Expressed emotion, is a measure of the family environment that is based on how the relatives of a psychiatric patient spontaneously talk about the patient. Theoretically, a high level of emotional expression in the home can worsen the prognosis in patients with mental illness, such as schizophrenia. Which of the following would be an example of high expressed emotion?
questions.explanation: Among people with a vulnerability to stress, high expressed emotions can cause relapse of psychiatric symptoms. The construct of Expressed Emotions comprises of Criticism, hostility, and emotional overinvolvement.

questions.question_text: Brown and Harris suggested that certain social factors increased the risk for women developing depressive illness. Which of the following is not a risk factor according to Brown and Harris?

options.text: 3 children under the age of 14 at home
Lack of employment outside the home

questions.explanation: The Brown and Harris model of depression holds that certain "vulnerability factors"--namely early maternal loss, lack of a confiding relationship, greater than three children under the age of 14 at home and unemployment--can interact with "provoking agents" to increase the risk of depression. Ref; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1188364/

questions.question_text: Joshua Bailey is a young boy who can appreciate that water poured from a tall, narrow glass into a short, wide one does not reduce in volume, despite its level seeming to be lower. Which of the following states of development is he most likely to be in?
questions.explanation: This is Piaget's famous test of conservation, which he described as being present in the concrete operational stage, when children will also demonstrate inductive reasoning. It occurs between the ages of 7-11 years.

questions.question_text: Kohlberg's stages of moral development theorise that moral reasoning, the basis for ethical behaviour, has six developmental stages, each more adequate at responding to moral dilemmas than its predecessor. Which of the following is true regarding Kohlberg's post conventional stage?

options.text: The approval of others is considered important

questions.explanation: The post-conventional level, also known as the principled level, is marked by a growing realization that individuals are separate entities from society, and that the individual's own perspective may take precedence over society's view; individuals may disobey rules inconsistent with their own principles. Some theorists have speculated that many people may never reach this level of abstract moral reasoning.

questions.question_text: Social learning theory or modelling is a theory of learning process and social behaviour which proposes that new behaviours can be acquired by observing others. Which of the following is not seen in modelling?
questions.explanation: The key steps in observational learning are identification, imitation and reinforcement, but everything begins with a role model demonstrating or modelling a behaviour, which is acquired and then performed by the observers. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3139552/

questions.question_text: For a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder-type 1, the individual should have experienced at least;

options.text: One hypomanic episode and one depressive episode
One manic episode and one depressive episode

questions.explanation: A diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder, Type I, requires the individual to have experienced at least one manic episode. Major depressive episodes are common in bipolar I disorder but are not required for the diagnosis of bipolar I disorder.. For bipolar II disorder, criteria should have been met for at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode.

questions.question_text: The brain develops throughout childhood and into early adulthood. Which of the following is most associated with adolescent brain development?
questions.explanation: Synaptic pruning, which includes both axon and dendrite completely decaying and dying off, is the process of synapse elimination that occurs between early childhood and the onset of puberty in many mammals, including humans. Pruning starts near the time of birth and continues into the mid-20s. It was traditionally considered to be complete by the time of sexual maturation but this has been discounted by MRI studies. The infant brain will increase in size by a factor of up to 5 by adulthood, reaching a final size of approximately 86 (± 8) billion neurons. Two factors contribute to this growth: the growth of synaptic connections between neurons, and the myelination of nerve fibers; the total number of neurons, however, remains the same. Pruning is influenced by environmental factors and is widely thought to represent learning. After adolescence, the volume of the synaptic connections decreases again due to synaptic pruning.

questions.question_text: Linguistic humour is based upon ambiguity in the use of words and phrases to produce amusing or absurd links or contexts. Which of the following stages of development is associated with the use of linguistic humour?
questions.explanation: Linguistic humour is thought to arise during the concrete operational stage of Piaget's theory of cognitive development as children are able to recognise and appreciate linguistic ambiguity and the humorous potential therein. (Ref: Honig AS. Humor development in children. Young children. 1988 May 1;43(4):60-73).

questions.question_text: Charlie Hodgkins is a young child who is placed in Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation test. He explores the room and shows interest in the stranger when they enter but is upset when his mother leaves. He seeks her out when she returns and is easily comforted. Which of the following types of attachment does this represent?
questions.explanation: This represents a secure attachment, whereby the child uses their caregiver as a secure base for exploring their surroundings, including the stranger. They are distressed when their caregiver leaves but seek them out for reassurance when they return. (Ref: Ainsworth MD and Bell SM. Attachment, exploration, and separation: Illustrated by the behavior of one-year- olds in a strange situation. Child Development; 1970;41:49-67). The correct answer is: Secure
